title: English Vocabulary 4 · Units 39–40
description: C1–C2 historical terminology, dynasties, evidence, military and social roles, and figurative historical language; precise distinctions among types of poverty, deprivation, inequality, wealth and financial-hardship idioms.
sourceNotice: Prepared for personal study from the user-supplied published reference material. Vocabulary targets and distinctions were checked against teaching pages, exercises and answer key. All translations, definitions, usage notes and example sentences were written independently; textbook paragraphs, exercises, tables and artwork are not reproduced.

audit.scope: Unit 39 sections A–D, historical and metaphorical meanings, exercises 39.1–39.4 and corresponding answer key; Unit 40 sections A–B including definitions, word-family contrasts and Common mistakes, exercises 40.1–40.4 and answer key.
audit.pronunciation: Selective broad British-English IPA is supplied for single words only when reasonably confident; empty IPA is intentional for many phrases. There are no phonetic recordings in this package.
audit.languagePolicy: All learner-facing information and metadata are in English, except Brazilian Portuguese translations in pt fields.
audit.reviewMethod: Reviewed the teaching and facing exercise pages with rendered page images and the relevant answer-key pages; checked core lexical targets, word families, figurative usages, grammar, register and historical qualifications. Authored new examples and translated to Brazilian Portuguese, then performed saved-JSON structural validation, unique-ID checks, provenance checks and static word-audio target linting.
audit.limitations: Real VocabLab browser import, text-to-speech and speech-recognition tests were not run. No MP3 files are included. Historical poverty thresholds in the source are not current and are intentionally not presented as current values. The book’s labels for historical periods and institutions are context-dependent.

units.title: Unit 39 — History: since the dawn of civilisation
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 39. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
units.category: History and society · historical evidence, periods, dynasties and metaphor
learningObjectives: Distinguish empire, kingdom and dynasty, and separate a hereditary heir from an eventual successor.
Discuss how historians and archaeologists interpret manuscripts and material evidence.
Name major historical periods, military categories and social roles with accurate register.
Recognise historical metaphors and word families including reign, succession, conquest and monarchy.

sectionsChecked: A · History – the great and the ordinary, numbered definitions and contextual examples
B · Historical eras and period labels
C · Military history and collective nouns
D · People and historical social roles

items.pt: arqueólogo; pesquisador de vestígios materiais do passado
items.section: A · History, dynasties and historical evidence
items.example: An archaeologist identified traces of domestic life beneath the ruined fortress.
items.note: An archaeologist studies material remains; a historian may work primarily with written records.

items.pt: arqueologia; estudo dos vestígios materiais de sociedades passadas
items.section: A · History, dynasties and historical evidence
items.example: Archaeology has revealed that the settlement was occupied for several centuries.
items.note: Abstract noun from archaeologist; distinct from history as a wider discipline.

items.section: A · History, dynasties and historical evidence
items.example: The remains of a civilisation emerged during construction work near the river.
items.note: Remains here refers to surviving physical traces of a former society.

items.section: A · History, dynasties and historical evidence
items.example: Archaeologists are investigating the origins of an ancient civilisation in the valley.
items.note: British spelling; American English uses civilization.

items.section: A · History, dynasties and historical evidence
items.example: The ruler expanded a vast empire through trade and military conquest.
items.note: An empire typically comprises territories or peoples under a single dominant power.

items.section: A · History, dynasties and historical evidence
items.example: The coastal kingdom developed strong commercial ties with neighbouring states.
items.note: Related to king; different from empire, which commonly includes several territories.

items.pt: dinastia; sequência de governantes da mesma família
items.section: A · History, dynasties and historical evidence
items.example: A new dynasty came to power after decades of political unrest.
items.note: Emphasises successive rulers belonging to one family, not simply a long period of government.

items.section: A · History, dynasties and historical evidence
items.example: People have traded goods across great distances since the dawn of civilisation.
items.note: Figurative dawn means the beginning of an era or process.

items.pt: reinado; período em que um monarca governa
items.section: A · History, dynasties and historical evidence
items.example: The archives document major reforms during the queen's reign.
items.note: As a noun, reign refers to the period or exercise of monarchical rule; compare rain, which sounds the same.

items.section: A · History, dynasties and historical evidence
items.example: The young monarch reigned over the kingdom for nearly four decades.
items.note: Verbal use of reign; it is intransitive with the optional preposition over.

items.section: A · History, dynasties and historical evidence
items.example: The emperor commissioned roads connecting the distant provinces.
items.note: A male monarch ruling an empire; compare emperor with king and empire with kingdom.

items.pt: herdeiro; pessoa com direito legal à sucessão
items.section: A · History, dynasties and historical evidence
items.example: The heir was still a child when the monarch died.
items.note: An heir has a legal or hereditary entitlement; the person who actually takes over is the successor. The h is silent.

items.pt: sucessor; quem assume um cargo ou função após alguém
items.section: A · History, dynasties and historical evidence
items.example: The president's successor immediately reversed several policies.
items.note: Does not necessarily imply an inherited right; a successor may be elected or appointed.

items.pt: suceder ao trono; assumir o trono por sucessão
items.section: A · History, dynasties and historical evidence
items.example: She succeeded to the throne following the sudden death of her father.
items.note: Succeed to the throne means become monarch; do not confuse it with succeed at a task.

items.pt: sucessão; passagem de poder ou posição
items.section: A · History, dynasties and historical evidence
items.example: The disputed succession created a prolonged crisis within the royal court.
items.note: The abstract noun connected with successor and succeed; can refer to a series or transfer of office.

items.pt: coroação; cerimônia de investidura de um monarca
items.section: A · History, dynasties and historical evidence
items.example: The coronation was attended by representatives from neighbouring kingdoms.
items.note: Ceremony in which a monarch is formally crowned.

items.pt: coroar; colocar oficialmente a coroa em alguém
items.section: A · History, dynasties and historical evidence
items.example: The new sovereign was crowned in a ceremony at the cathedral.
items.note: The verb crown refers to formal investiture; also a noun for the symbolic headpiece.

items.section: A · History, dynasties and historical evidence
items.example: The conquest reshaped the language and institutions of the region.
items.note: Refers to gaining control through military force; related to conquer and conqueror.

items.section: A · History, dynasties and historical evidence
items.example: The invading army failed to conquer the mountainous territory.
items.note: More forceful than discover or explore; means defeat and take control.

items.pt: conquistador militar; aquele que conquista territórios
items.section: A · History, dynasties and historical evidence
items.example: Later generations remembered the conqueror as both a strategist and a ruthless ruler.
items.note: Person noun formed from conquer; not equivalent to an explorer.

items.pt: manuscrito; texto originalmente escrito à mão
items.section: A · History, dynasties and historical evidence
items.example: A damaged manuscript provides the earliest surviving account of the conflict.
items.note: Historically a text written by hand; in publishing, manuscript can also mean an author's unpublished text.

items.pt: tabuleta de pedra; placa de pedra gravada
items.section: A · History, dynasties and historical evidence
items.example: The stone tablet preserved records of payments made to the temple.
items.note: Ancient writing medium; tablet here is not an electronic device.

items.pt: camponês; trabalhador rural de baixa posição social histórica
items.section: A · History, dynasties and historical evidence
items.example: The peasant paid rent to the local landowner in grain.
items.note: Historically a low-status agricultural worker or small farmer; can be disparaging if used of people today.

items.pt: trabalhador braçal; operário de trabalho manual não especializado
items.section: A · History, dynasties and historical evidence
items.example: Labourers carried stone from the quarry to the building site.
items.note: British spelling; often means a worker performing physical, frequently unskilled work.

items.pt: trabalho; esforço físico ou atividade laboral
items.section: A · History, dynasties and historical evidence
items.example: The construction required years of sustained labour.
items.note: Noun related to labourer; also a verb meaning work hard. British spelling.

items.section: A · History, dynasties and historical evidence
items.example: Evidence of migration appears in changes to pottery and settlement patterns.
items.note: Movement of people from one region to another; related to migrant and migrate.

items.pt: migrante; pessoa que se desloca para viver em outro lugar
items.section: A · History, dynasties and historical evidence
items.example: Migrants brought new farming techniques to the growing town.
items.note: Person noun; may describe internal or international movement.

items.pt: migrar; mudar de região ou país
items.section: A · History, dynasties and historical evidence
items.example: Some communities migrated towards fertile land during the prolonged drought.
items.note: Intransitive verb, often migrate to or from a place.

items.pt: um mínimo vestígio de prova; um fragmento de evidência
items.section: A · History, dynasties and historical evidence
items.example: Investigators found only a shred of evidence linking the objects to the settlement.
items.note: Shred implies a very small amount; often used in no shred of evidence to emphasise complete absence.

items.section: A · History, dynasties and historical evidence
items.example: Researchers disagreed about how to interpret the historical evidence.
items.note: Interpret suggests explaining the meaning of surviving material, not merely recording it.

items.section: B · Historical eras
items.example: The exhibition examines navigation techniques in ancient Mediterranean societies.
items.note: Used of remote historical periods; does not simply mean a few years old.

items.section: B · Historical eras
items.example: The earliest artefacts in the collection date from the Stone Age.
items.note: Prehistoric period characterised by widespread use of stone tools; an era name, not a particular dynasty.

items.section: B · Historical eras
items.example: Bronze Age settlements often contained objects made from copper alloys.
items.note: Historical period associated with widespread bronze technology.

items.section: B · Historical eras
items.example: The Iron Age saw major changes in tools and warfare in many regions.
items.note: Period associated with the increased use of iron; its dates vary by region.

items.section: B · Historical eras
items.example: The archaeologists uncovered the foundations of a medieval monastery.
items.note: Historical adjective for the Middle Ages; sometimes metaphorically used to criticise very old-fashioned attitudes.

items.pt: Renascimento; movimento cultural e artístico de renovação
items.section: B · Historical eras
items.example: Renaissance painters experimented with perspective and anatomy.
items.note: In European history, a period of renewed activity in the arts and learning; also figuratively a revival.

items.pt: era pré-colonial; período anterior à colonização
items.section: B · Historical eras
items.example: The exhibition focuses on artistic traditions from the pre-colonial era.
items.note: Relative to a region's colonial history; do not assume the period is identical everywhere.

items.pt: era pós-colonial; período posterior ao domínio colonial
items.section: B · Historical eras
items.example: Scholars debate how institutions changed in the post-colonial era.
items.note: Contrasts with pre-colonial; the post-colonial label can also refer to critical study of colonial legacies.

items.pt: infantaria; soldados que combatem a pé
items.section: C · Military history
items.example: The infantry crossed the valley before the cavalry arrived.
items.note: Collective uncountable noun for soldiers fighting on foot; not normally an individual infantry.

items.section: C · Military history
items.example: The cavalry moved rapidly towards the exposed flank of the army.
items.note: Historical mounted soldiers; a collective uncountable noun.

items.pt: armadura completa; conjunto de peças protetoras de metal
items.section: C · Military history
items.example: A carefully restored suit of armour stands near the entrance to the museum.
items.note: British spelling armour; the suit is protective equipment rather than a uniform.

items.pt: biga; carro de duas rodas puxado por cavalos
items.section: C · Military history
items.example: The ceremonial chariot was decorated with gold and painted wood.
items.note: Two-wheeled horse-drawn vehicle used for transport, racing or warfare in antiquity.

items.pt: galeão; grande navio à vela antigo
items.section: C · Military history
items.example: The museum commissioned a scale model of a sixteenth-century galleon.
items.note: Large multi-masted sailing ship particularly associated with early modern maritime history.

items.pt: senhor da guerra; líder militar que controla um território
items.section: D · Historical roles and social groups
items.example: A powerful warlord controlled the mountain passes and surrounding settlements.
items.note: A military leader exercising political or territorial power, often outside a stable central state.

items.pt: pessoa escravizada; escravo em contexto histórico
items.section: D · Historical roles and social groups
items.example: Historical records show that enslaved people were forced to work in the fields.
items.note: The source uses slave for a person legally treated as property; enslaved person is often preferred in contemporary discussion.

items.section: D · Historical roles and social groups
items.example: The archive documents resistance to slavery over several generations.
items.note: Abstract noun for the institution or condition of enslavement.

items.pt: governante; pessoa que exerce poder político
items.section: D · Historical roles and social groups
items.example: The ruler introduced a new system of taxation across the territory.
items.note: General term for a person exercising authority over a state or territory.

items.section: D · Historical roles and social groups
items.example: Several monarchs ruled the region before the republic was established.
items.note: Verb related to ruler; a rule can also mean a regulation, a different sense.

items.pt: explorador; pessoa que realiza expedições para conhecer lugares
items.section: D · Historical roles and social groups
items.example: The explorer's maps changed European knowledge of the coast.
items.note: Historical term for a traveller investigating unfamiliar places; not a synonym for conqueror.

items.pt: mercador; comerciante atacadista ou de longa distância
items.section: D · Historical roles and social groups
items.example: Merchants carried textiles and spices between distant trading ports.
items.note: Particularly historical term for people involved in commerce, often on a large scale.

items.section: D · Historical roles and social groups
items.example: The monarch retained a ceremonial role after the constitutional reforms.
items.note: Gender-neutral noun for king or queen; connected with monarchy.

items.pt: monarquia; sistema político chefiado por um monarca
items.section: D · Historical roles and social groups
items.example: The country remained a constitutional monarchy for more than a century.
items.note: Political system rather than the individual monarch.

items.pt: nobreza; grupo de pessoas de alta posição social hereditária
items.section: D · Historical roles and social groups
items.example: Members of the nobility held much of the region's farmland.
items.note: Collective term for an elite hereditary social class; not simply everyone who is wealthy.

items.pt: como um galeão com todas as velas abertas; figura de porte imponente
items.section: Exercises · Historical metaphors
items.example: The actress entered the hall like a galleon in full sail, commanding everyone's attention.
items.note: Figurative comparison suggesting stately, imposing movement or appearance.

items.pt: atravessar a couraça emocional de alguém; vencer suas defesas
items.section: Exercises · Historical metaphors
items.example: It took years for even close friends to penetrate his emotional armour.
items.note: Armour is metaphorical emotional protection, not literal metal clothing.

items.pt: renascimento do interesse; retomada intensa de interesse
items.section: Exercises · Historical metaphors
items.example: The discovery prompted a renaissance of interest in traditional astronomy.
items.note: Lower-case renaissance denotes revival; distinguish from the historical Renaissance.

items.pt: refém da tradição; pessoa presa aos costumes
items.section: Exercises · Historical metaphors
items.example: The curator argued that the exhibition should not be a slave to tradition.
items.note: A figurative sense of slave meaning excessively controlled by a habit or convention.

items.section: Exercises · Historical metaphors
items.example: The columnist criticised the policy as reflecting a medieval attitude to women's rights.
items.note: Figurative and disapproving, meaning extremely old-fashioned; different from literal historical medieval.

units.title: Unit 40 — The haves and the have-nots
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 40. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
units.category: Society and economics · poverty, social deprivation and material inequality
learningObjectives: Distinguish absolute, relative, extreme and human poverty without treating historical thresholds as current.
Use precise terms for multidimensional deprivation, nutrition, literacy, shelter and sanitation.
Contrast impoverished, destitute, affluent and classed as poor according to degree and register.
Use fixed expressions such as make ends meet, on the breadline, live from hand to mouth and tighten your belt.

sectionsChecked: A · Definitions of poverty, poverty typology, numbered explanations and contextual qualifications
B · Wealth and poverty expressions and Common mistakes
Exercises 40.1–40.4, social-meaning contrasts and relevant answer key

items.section: A · Defining poverty and social deprivation
items.example: Fundamentally, the disagreement concerns access to basic public services.
items.note: Adverb marking an essential point or underlying principle, rather than a minor detail.

items.section: A · Defining poverty and social deprivation
items.example: The report links persistent inequality to the denial of opportunities in early childhood.
items.note: Denial here means withholding or refusing access; different from denying an accusation.

items.section: A · Defining poverty and social deprivation
items.example: The committee condemned the treatment as a violation of human dignity.
items.note: Formal human-rights collocation; violation means an infringement of a right or principle.

items.section: A · Defining poverty and social deprivation
items.example: Safe accommodation and respectful treatment are essential to human dignity.
items.note: Dignity refers to the inherent worth of people, not merely social status.

items.section: A · Defining poverty and social deprivation
items.example: Economists use defined material thresholds to measure absolute poverty.
items.note: Poverty assessed against a specified minimum standard rather than comparison with neighbours.

items.section: A · Defining poverty and social deprivation
items.example: A family may experience relative poverty despite living above an absolute poverty threshold.
items.note: Poverty defined in comparison with income or living standards in a particular society.

items.section: A · Defining poverty and social deprivation
items.example: The programme aims to reduce extreme poverty in remote rural districts.
items.note: In the source, this refers to living below a poverty line; actual thresholds change by year and institution.

items.section: A · Defining poverty and social deprivation
items.example: The study of human poverty includes access to education, health and safe housing.
items.note: Wider than income alone; focuses on several forms of deprivation.

items.pt: linha de pobreza; limite de renda de referência
items.section: A · Defining poverty and social deprivation
items.example: The agency revised its poverty line to reflect updated measurement criteria.
items.note: A defined threshold for poverty classification, not a single timeless monetary amount.

items.section: A · Defining poverty and social deprivation
items.example: Many households remained below the poverty line despite increases in employment.
items.note: Fixed collocation with below; the precise threshold depends on the measurement system.

items.section: A · Defining poverty and social deprivation
items.example: The meaning of adequate housing depends partly on the local social context.
items.note: Context here means the surrounding economic and social circumstances.

items.section: A · Defining poverty and social deprivation
items.example: The policy paper compares income inequality across different regions.
items.note: Unequal distribution of income, which is not identical to the overall level of poverty.

items.section: A · Defining poverty and social deprivation
items.example: After losing his inheritance, the former official lived in penury.
items.note: Formal, literary noun for severe poverty; not a common everyday synonym for low income.

items.section: A · Defining poverty and social deprivation
items.example: The emergency response prioritised shelter, clean water and food.
items.note: As a basic human need, shelter means protection and a place to live.

items.pt: nutrição; alimentação adequada do ponto de vista nutricional
items.section: A · Defining poverty and social deprivation
items.example: The initiative focuses on maternal nutrition and access to nutritious food.
items.note: Describes nourishment or the process of obtaining nutrients; not automatically the same as diet.

items.section: A · Defining poverty and social deprivation
items.example: Children who were severely malnourished received specialist care.
items.note: Adjective describing inadequate nutrition, which can involve deficiencies and not just insufficient calories.

items.section: A · Defining poverty and social deprivation
items.example: Prolonged malnourishment can affect physical and cognitive development.
items.note: Noun corresponding to malnourished; also called malnutrition.

items.section: A · Defining poverty and social deprivation
items.example: The researchers examined malnutrition alongside preventable infections.
items.note: Common noun for inadequate or imbalanced nutrition; overlaps with malnourishment.

items.pt: alfabetização; capacidade de ler e escrever
items.section: A · Defining poverty and social deprivation
items.example: Adult literacy improved after the community opened evening classes.
items.note: Ability to read and write; the opposite state is illiteracy.

items.pt: analfabeto; que não sabe ler nem escrever
items.section: A · Defining poverty and social deprivation
items.example: The survey counted adults who were unable to read and were classified as illiterate.
items.note: Adjective for inability to read or write; avoid treating it as a synonym for unintelligent.

items.section: A · Defining poverty and social deprivation
items.example: The initiative seeks to reduce illiteracy through accessible adult education.
items.note: Abstract noun for the condition of being unable to read and write.

items.pt: saneamento; infraestrutura de higiene e esgoto
items.section: A · Defining poverty and social deprivation
items.example: Inadequate sanitation has contributed to contaminated drinking water in the settlement.
items.note: Basic systems for hygienic waste disposal and sewage handling; not simply personal cleanliness.

items.pt: privado de recursos essenciais; em situação de carência
items.section: A · Defining poverty and social deprivation
items.example: The scheme provides additional support to children from deprived communities.
items.note: Deprived can refer to material or non-material needs; not identical to destitute.

items.section: A · Defining poverty and social deprivation
items.example: Long-term deprivation can limit access to education and healthcare.
items.note: The condition of lacking necessities or opportunities; related to deprived.

items.section: B · Wealth, hardship and idiomatic expressions
items.example: Under the revised criteria, more households were classed as poor.
items.note: Class as or be classed as means officially categorise; not the same as belong to a social class.

items.section: B · Wealth, hardship and idiomatic expressions
items.example: The district's relative affluence concealed sharp differences between households.
items.note: Formal noun for wealth and material prosperity; the adjective is affluent.

items.section: B · Wealth, hardship and idiomatic expressions
items.example: The affluent suburb has a far higher average income than the surrounding area.
items.note: Formal adjective for a wealthy person, family or community.

items.pt: os super-ricos; a parcela extremamente rica da população
items.section: B · Wealth, hardship and idiomatic expressions
items.example: The report considers how the super-rich influence the housing market.
items.note: Collective nominalised adjective; describes exceptionally wealthy people.

items.pt: viver na linha da miséria; sobreviver com o mínimo
items.section: B · Wealth, hardship and idiomatic expressions
items.example: Many pensioners lived on the breadline before the benefit increase.
items.note: Informal expression for having barely enough money to meet basic needs.

items.pt: conseguir fechar as contas; fazer o dinheiro render até o fim do mês
items.section: B · Wealth, hardship and idiomatic expressions
items.example: Rising rent made it difficult for the family to make ends meet.
items.note: Idiom for having sufficient income to cover necessary expenses.

items.section: B · Wealth, hardship and idiomatic expressions
items.example: The charity established a clinic in a poverty-stricken district.
items.note: Strongly negative compound adjective, often before a noun such as area or community.

items.section: B · Wealth, hardship and idiomatic expressions
items.example: The organisation provides legal advice to impoverished families.
items.note: Formal adjective for made poor or living without adequate financial means; less extreme than destitute.

items.pt: indigente; em miséria extrema; sem meios de subsistência
items.section: B · Wealth, hardship and idiomatic expressions
items.example: After the disaster, some displaced families were left destitute.
items.note: Stronger than poor or impoverished: lacking the resources required to survive.

items.section: B · Wealth, hardship and idiomatic expressions
items.example: The report describes the risk of destitution among families without secure housing.
items.note: Abstract noun corresponding to destitute.

items.pt: viver da mão para a boca; viver sem conseguir poupar
items.section: B · Wealth, hardship and idiomatic expressions
items.example: For years they lived from hand to mouth, spending their wages on immediate needs.
items.note: Fixed idiom meaning have only enough income for basic day-to-day survival.

items.pt: o dinheiro está curto; o orçamento está apertado
items.section: B · Wealth, hardship and idiomatic expressions
items.example: Money is tight this month, so we are postponing non-essential purchases.
items.note: Everyday expression for having little money available.

items.section: B · Wealth, hardship and idiomatic expressions
items.example: We will have to tighten our belts until the business recovers.
items.note: Idiom meaning spend less, especially because income has decreased.

items.section: B · Wealth, hardship and idiomatic expressions
items.example: Applicants in the lowest income bracket qualify for the larger subsidy.
items.note: A band of incomes with specified upper and lower limits.

items.section: B · Wealth, hardship and idiomatic expressions
items.example: Residents in the lowest income bracket face the greatest rent burden.
items.note: A fixed comparative collocation; income bracket alone may refer to any band.

items.section: B · Wealth, hardship and idiomatic expressions
items.example: The documentary examines unequal access to public transport among the rich and the poor.
items.note: Collective nominalised adjectives take the, without adding plural -s: not the riches or the poors.

items.section: B · Wealth, hardship and idiomatic expressions
items.example: A child may be materially comfortable yet deprived of affection.
items.note: The adjective deprived can describe emotional and social needs, not only financial ones.
